name: Threadline Co. Denim Chore Coat
description:
Threadline Co. is a small independent label operating out of a storefront in the Tier 2 manufacturing district, making garments from deadstock and reclaimed fabric. The Denim Chore Coat is their signature piece — a boxy, hip-length work jacket in 12-oz selvedge denim, with four front pockets, a clean collar, and a single-button closure at the throat. The denim is raw and stiff when new, fading and softening over months of wear into something personal. Threadline offers it in indigo (standard), black-washed, and a natural undyed ecru that takes dye and grime alike.

This jacket has significant underground cachet. It is recognizable to people who know it and invisible to people who do not, which is part of the appeal. Artists, musicians, fabricators, and Tier 2-to-3 crossover types wear it. It gets pins, hand-stitched patches, and paint on it. It is not trying to compete with corp brands — it has nothing to prove to them.
what_it_says: You know what this is and you bought it from a person, not a terminal. You probably have opinions about manufacturing and you are not wrong.
story_hooks: A specific run of Threadline chore coats was made from denim bolted from a corp warehouse during a labor action — wearing one is a political statement to those who know
The Threadline storefront is facing a buyout from a Tier 4 lifestyle conglomerate; the founder is looking for help making it go away
A character needs to blend into a Tier 2 creative scene quickly; the right person tells them to get a Threadline coat before anything else

physical_description.visual_profile: A boxy, utilitarian silhouette that sits at the hip with a relaxed, unadorned presence. The jacket reads as deliberately understated — no logos, no chrome accents, no aspirational sheen. It has the honest geometry of workwear from a century prior, adapted without irony into contemporary streetwear. On the wearer, it creates a grounded, thoughtful impression: someone who values material authenticity and doesn't perform for tier systems.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and roomy through the shoulders and chest, with a straight drop to the hip. Not oversized, but untatered — there's room to move, to layer underneath, to work in. The sleeves are long enough to break slightly at the wrist. The overall effect is comfortable rather than tailored.
physical_description.primary_material: 12-ounce Japanese selvedge denim, raw or finished depending on colorway. Deadstock and reclaimed sourcing means slight variations in weave density and hand. Threads are thick and visible; the fabric has weight and structure.
physical_description.texture: Heavy, with a pronounced slub. Raw indigo is stiff and slightly nubbled; aged versions develop a soft nap and visible creasing along movement points (elbows, folds, seams). Black-washed and ecru variants have a more uniform finish but retain the fabric's characteristic roughness. All versions invite patina.
physical_description.color_scheme: Three options: deep indigo (fades to pale blue-grey at stress points with wear), solid black-washed (develops faded creases over time), or natural ecru (yellows and dirties into warm ochre and grey). All are matte and grounded — no shine, no coating.
physical_description.closures: Single button at the throat in matte bronze or bone, depending on run. Four front pockets with simple bar-tack reinforcement at stress points. No zippers, no magnetic snaps — purely mechanical, repairable closures.
distinctive_features: Visible selvedge edge on inner cuffs — a marker of intentional fabric choice
Four deep front pockets with reinforced corners — designed for tool carry and customization
Raw or minimal seaming — visible topstitching in contrasting thread on some runs
Blank canvas quality: the jacket is naked of branding, begging for pins, patches, hand-stitched marks, paint, wear
Slight irregularities in weave and dye indicative of deadstock sourcing
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2–3 crossover. The independent label and reclaimed sourcing read as Tier 2 maker ethics, but the price point and street credibility among artists and fabricators positions it as aspirational Tier 3 — working-class with cultural cache.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by people who make things: fabricators, musicians, artists, DIY tech enthusiasts, small-shop operators. It signals anti-corporate taste without being aggressively countercultural. To people outside its subculture, it's invisible — just a denim jacket. To people inside, it's a statement of alignment with independent production, material respect, and willingness to let a garment tell the story of its wear.
physical_description.condition_typical: Ranges dramatically: new jackets are stiff and pristine; worn examples show deep indigo fade at elbows, thighs, and creases, softened fabric, visible creasing, and often a layer of customization — pins from local venues, hand-stitched patches, paint marks, bleach splatter, grease stains from work. The jacket gets more interesting with age.

image_prompt: A worn Threadline Co. Denim Chore Coat displayed on a dark mannequin or draped over a workbench in a dimly-lit fabrication studio. The indigo has faded to pale grey-blue at the elbows and chest; several hand-stitched fabric patches and enamel pins decorate the front and sleeves — references to underground music venues and fabricator collectives. Moody, cool lighting from a side angle highlights the selvedge edge and the texture of the denim. Urban backdrop: exposed brick wall or metal shelving with tools and scrap materials. Shot in 2x3 portrait orientation. Neo-noir urban aesthetic, no neon, documentary realism. --ar 2:3 --v 6
